subject: chemistry
question_text: Write a note on the anomalous behaviour of beryllium.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.89, chapter 7 s-BLOCK ELEMENTS, SAQ question 41. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. STRUCTURE: the card gives the causes first (small atomic and ionic size, high polarising power, high ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity, no vacant d orbitals in the valence shell) and then the three consequences that follow from them — largely covalent and easily hydrolysed compounds, a maximum coordination number of four, and an amphoteric oxide and hydroxide. The two example ions carried as extra content, [BeF₄]²⁻ for coordination number four and [Mg(H₂O)₆]²⁺ for coordination number six, are standard values and are not taken from the source book; a teacher should confirm them before they are relied on.

steps.label: Why beryllium is different
lines: Beryllium is the first member of group 2
and differs from the rest of the group.
1. its very small atomic and ionic size,
2. its high polarising power, that is a
3. its high ionisation enthalpy and high
4. no vacant d orbitals in its valence
steps.why: Every difference written below comes from one of these four points, so they are set out first. A small ion carrying a double charge pulls on electrons far harder than magnesium does, and having only 2s and 2p orbitals available fixes how many groups can bond to beryllium.
common_mistakes: Giving only the small size. The high polarising power and the absence of d orbitals are separate reasons.
Saying beryllium has d orbitals in its valence shell. Its valence shell is the second shell, which has no d orbitals.
steps.memory_tip: Small size, high polarising power, high ionisation enthalpy, no d orbitals.
steps.margin_note: Write the reasons before the differences; each difference then follows from one of them.

steps.why: A small cation with a double charge distorts the anion so far that the electrons are shared rather than transferred, which is Fajans' rule applied to beryllium. Hydrolysis follows from the same covalent character: a covalent halide such as BeCl₂ reacts with water instead of dissolving unchanged as an ionic salt does.
common_mistakes: Writing that beryllium compounds are ionic like those of the rest of the group. They are largely covalent.
Leaving out hydrolysis. The covalent compounds of beryllium are easily hydrolysed by water.
steps.memory_tip: Small ion, strong pull, shared electrons: the compounds of beryllium are covalent.
steps.margin_note: Fajans' rule may be named here; the small size with a double charge is the reason.

steps.label: Coordination number four
lines: The valence shell of beryllium has only
So beryllium holds at most four groups
The other members of group 2 have vacant
d orbitals and reach a coordination
steps.why: The number of groups a metal can bond is limited by the number of orbitals available to it. Beryllium's second shell has no d orbitals, so four is its limit, while magnesium and the metals below it can use d orbitals and take six.
common_mistakes: Writing a coordination number of six for beryllium. Four is its maximum.
Giving no example. One ion such as [BeF₄]²⁻ makes the limit clear.
steps.memory_tip: One 2s and three 2p make four orbitals, so four is the limit for beryllium.
steps.margin_note: State the orbital count; the coordination number four follows from it.

steps.label: Amphoteric oxide and hydroxide
lines: The oxides and hydroxides of the other
steps.why: This is the clearest single difference between beryllium and the rest of its group, so it makes a strong closing line. The resemblance to aluminium is worth one sentence because it comes from the same small size and high charge that caused every other difference.
common_mistakes: Writing that BeO is basic like MgO. BeO is amphoteric while MgO is basic.
Stopping after the covalent character. The amphoteric oxide and hydroxide are a separate difference and are the best known one.
steps.memory_tip: Beryllium is the one metal in group 2 whose oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric.
steps.margin_note: Close with the amphoteric oxide and hydroxide, the sharpest difference in the group.

insider_note: Give the causes first and the differences after them; a note that lists differences with no reason behind them reads as memorised rather than understood.
